To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
both the functions of the I/O curves for evoked EPSCs and the functions of I/0 curves for the evoked IPSCs are changed in the DG of rats with acute inflammatory or chronic neuropathic conditions.

the functions of both excitatory and the inhibitory synaptic transmission are altered in the dentate gyruses under different pathological pain condition, and the changes in inhibitory controls are more significant than those of excitatory controls.
the functions of I-O curves for evoked eIPSCs and mIPSCs are gained under inflammatory condition but reduced under neuropathice condition.

the changes of synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus under inflammatory pain condition and neuropathic pain, and the results provide a new understanding of the pathophysiology of the pain and a new therapeutic approach for the pain.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
both inflammatory and neuropathic pain causes imbalance of excitation-inhibition at the synaptic level in the dentate gyris.

the synaptic transmission and modulation in the dentate gyruses of the two different pain conditions (acute inflammatory and chronic neuropathy) are both homeostatically and allostatically modulated, however, the mechanisms of the modulation are different in the two conditions.

both inflammatory and neuropathic pain causes synaptic homeostasis and allostasis in the DG, but the mechanisms underlying the synaptic homeostasis/allostasis may differ between the two pain conditions, which may have implications for the treatment of pain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DG granule cell network undergoes synaptic homeostatic and/or allostatic changes to maintain the balance between excitation and the inhibitory control under different pain conditions.
